<explanation>
Based on the file structure and the contents of the README, this project is a Go-based, command-line tool designed to lint Terraform files with a pluggable architecture. The system design diagram should capture several layers and components that work together to:
 • Parse and analyze Terraform configurations
 • Execute linting rules (both built-in and plugin-supplied)
 • Provide output in various formats
 • Optionally offer integrations like language server capabilities and Docker usage

Below is a detailed rundown for drawing the most accurate and comprehensive system design diagram:

1. Identify the Main Components:

 a. Command-Line Interface (CLI)
  – Represented by the “cmd” directory (files such as cli.go, init.go, version.go, etc.).
  – It handles user input, initialization, and the overall execution flow.
  – This component triggers plugin initialization, configuration loading, and subsequent linter operations.

 b. Configuration & Core Linting Engine
  – Located partly in the “tflint” package and the “terraform” directory.
  – Responsible for loading configurations (as shown in files like config.go), parsing Terraform files (under terraform/parser.go and related files), and executing the linting logic.
  – Acts as the heart of the application by evaluating rules, managing module references, and reporting issues.

 c. Plugin Framework
  – Found in the “plugin” directory and related stub-generator sources.
  – Manages discovery, installation, checksum verification (e.g. checksum.go), and executing external plugins.
  – Enables extensibility so that linting rules can be added or overridden (notice the bundled plugin mechanism for rulesets such as AWS, Azure, GCP, etc.).
  – The configuration files (like .tflint.hcl examples in the README) indicate how users add/enable their plugins.

 d. Formatter Layer
  – Present in the “formatter” directory.
  – Converts internal lint diagnostics into various user-facing formats: JSON, checkstyle, junit, compact, and SARIF.
  – Should be represented as a component that accepts results from the linting core and outputs the final report.

 e. Language Server
  – Implemented in the “langserver” directory.
  – Provides IDE integrations by enabling real-time linting data and other communications via protocols (files include text_document_did_open.go, handler.go, etc.).
  – Mark it as an optional integration service that is invoked when users run the tool with the “--langserver” flag.

 f. Integration and Testing Infrastructure
  – The “integrationtest” directory contains various test scenarios and sample Terraform configurations.
  – Though primarily for testing, this outlines the expected flows from user input through parsing and linting to output.
  – You might indicate this in the diagram as a layer used for system validation rather than production flow.

 g. Supporting and Build Infrastructure
  – Acknowledge the presence of Dockerfile, Makefile, CI/CD workflows (in .github/workflows), and various shell scripts.
  – These files indicate how the application is built, containerized, and released. Mark them as supporting components that feed into the continuous integration/deployment pipeline.

2. Define Relationships and Interactions:

 – The CLI component acts as the entry point. It interacts with the configuration loader which, in turn, initializes the linting engine.
 – The linting engine consults the Plugin Framework to load built-in and user-supplied rules.
 – Once rules are evaluated on Terraform configurations (using parsing and evaluation logic from the “terraform” packages), the results are passed to the Formatter for output.
 – Optionally, if running in language server mode, the langserver component will interface with an IDE, receiving real-time file changes and providing feedback.
 – Surround the main process with integration flows (and testing feedback loops) that verify the rule engine’s integrity.
 – Also, highlight the CI/CD components (Docker, GitHub workflows) that orchestrate builds, tests, and releases.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:

 – Plugin Architecture: Emphasize that TFLint is designed to be extended via plugins, hence use a “plugin manager” or “modular” component that supports dynamic loading and validation (e.g., checksum/signer verification).
 – Layered Design: Separate interaction concerns (CLI, language server) from business logic (parsing, evaluation) and output (formatter).
 – Extensibility & Reusability: Indicate that the engine is built to support multiple Terraform providers by enabling external rulesets.
 – Testing/Integration: Clearly mark the usage of integration tests that simulate real-world scenarios and validate end-to-end flows.

4. Tailor Your Diagram for a Full-Stack CLI Tool with Plugins:

 – Create distinct boxes for each main subsystem (CLI, Core Engine, Plugin Manager, Formatter, Language Server).
 – Use directional arrows to indicate data flow:
  • From CLI → Configuration Loader → Core Engine.
  • From Core Engine → Plugin Framework for rule retrieval.
  • From Core Engine → Formatter to output results.
  • Optionally, Flow between CLI/Configuration Loader and Language Server when in IDE integration mode.
 – Optionally add side boxes for build and deployment pipelines (GitHub workflows, Docker containers) that wrap around the source code.

5. Provide Guidelines for Diagram Presentation:

 – Clear labels: Ensure each component’s name is clearly marked (e.g., “CLI”, “Plugin Manager”, “Lint Engine”).
 – Directional arrows: Use arrows to show the flow from user input to configuration, linting evaluation, plugin interaction, and final output.
 – Color Coding/Shapes: Use different colors or shapes to differentiate core modules (engine, parser, evaluator), auxiliary components (formatter, language server), and external systems (CI/CD pipelines, Docker).
 – Annotations: Include brief notes in the diagram to highlight key decisions (like the pluggable architecture design and layered separation).

By capturing these elements—each of the main directories and their responsibilities, the overall flow from configuration input to linting output, the dynamic loading and verification of plugins, and the testing/integration support—you will provide a comprehensive, accurate system design diagram that clearly represents TFLint’s architecture as detailed in the file tree and README.
</explanation>
